candidates.topic: The Baychimo — Ghost Ship That Sailed Alone for 38 Years
candidates.teaser: A cargo ship disappeared in the Arctic in 1931 — and kept being spotted, crewless, for nearly four decades after.
candidates.video_title: The Ghost Ship That Sailed Alone for 38 Years
candidates.video_description: The SS Baychimo was abandoned in an Arctic blizzard in 1931. Its crew escaped, but the ship didn't sink — it kept drifting, unmanned, spotted by sailors and Inuit hunters for 38 years. No one ever reclaimed it.
candidates.script: A ship was abandoned in the Arctic in 1931 — and then it sailed on alone for 38 years. The SS Baychimo got trapped in pack ice near Alaska. The crew escaped, expecting it to sink. It didn't. For nearly four decades, Inuit hunters and passing sailors kept spotting it, completely empty, drifting through frozen waters. The last confirmed sighting was 1969. The wreck has never been found. So where is it now?

candidates.topic: The Tardigrade — Only Animal That Can Survive in Outer Space
candidates.teaser: There's a creature smaller than a grain of sand that can survive boiling water, deep vacuum, and direct radiation in open space.
candidates.video_title: The Tiny Animal That Survives Open Space
candidates.video_description: Tardigrades, microscopic animals under 1mm long, have been exposed directly to the vacuum and radiation of outer space and returned alive. They survive by entering a death-like state called cryptobiosis, reducing their metabolism to 0.01% of normal.
candidates.script: Scientists shot live animals directly into outer space — no suit, no capsule — and they survived. Tardigrades, less than one millimeter long, were exposed to the full vacuum and solar radiation of open space for ten days. When researchers brought them back, most were still alive. They do it by folding themselves into a glass-like shell and dropping their metabolism to nearly zero. They've also survived 300 years frozen in Antarctic moss. What exactly is keeping them alive?

candidates.topic: The Tanganyika Laughter Epidemic — Mass Hysteria That Closed Schools for Months
candidates.teaser: In 1962, a laughing fit started in a single classroom — and within weeks, an entire region couldn't stop.
candidates.video_title: The Laughing Epidemic That Shut Down Schools
candidates.video_description: In January 1962 in Tanzania, three schoolgirls began laughing uncontrollably. The laughter spread to 95 students, then to surrounding villages. Schools were forced to close for months. No medical cause was ever identified.
candidates.script: In January 1962, three girls in a Tanzanian boarding school started laughing — and couldn't stop for sixteen days. The laughter spread to 95 of the 159 students. Then it jumped to nearby villages, infecting over a thousand people. Schools were shut down for months. Victims reported crying, fainting, and rashes alongside the uncontrollable laughter. Doctors examined everyone and found absolutely nothing wrong. Mass hysteria, they said. But does that actually explain anything?

candidates.topic: The Loneliest Tree — Pando, the Single Organism Covering 43 Hectares
candidates.teaser: What looks like an entire forest in Utah is actually one single living organism — and it's dying.
candidates.video_title: This Entire Forest Is One Single Living Thing
candidates.video_description: Pando, a grove of quaking aspen trees in Utah, is genetically a single organism connected by one massive root system. It covers 43 hectares, weighs 6 million kilograms, and is estimated to be 80,000 years old. It is currently shrinking.
candidates.script: That forest in Utah isn't a forest. Every single one of those 47,000 trees is the same organism, all connected underground by one root system. It's called Pando. It weighs six million kilograms, making it the heaviest known living thing on Earth. It's also estimated to be 80,000 years old — it was alive before modern humans left Africa. And right now, for the first time in its existence, it's shrinking. Scientists aren't sure we can stop it.

candidates.topic: The Uncanny Valley — Why Almost-Human Faces Feel Deeply Wrong
candidates.teaser: The closer a robot or image looks to a real human face, the more deeply disturbing it feels — and there's a precise graph that explains why.
candidates.video_title: Why Almost-Human Faces Feel Deeply Wrong
candidates.video_description: The Uncanny Valley is a 1970 robotics theory by Masahiro Mori showing that as artificial faces approach — but don't quite reach — human realism, they trigger intense unease. The effect is so powerful it influences Hollywood CGI, surgical planning, and AI avatar design.
candidates.script: The closer a robot looks to a real human, the more people want to run. In 1970, roboticist Masahiro Mori mapped it on a graph — affinity rises as faces get more human-like, then suddenly drops into a valley of deep revulsion just before reaching perfect realism. Brain scans show why: your threat-detection system fires when something looks almost right but not quite. Hollywood spent millions learning this the hard way with 2004's 'The Polar Express.' So does your brain ever fully trust an AI face?
